items.title: The $103,265 Price Tag: Inside Trump's Push to Make His H-1B Visa Fee Permanent
items.body:
## A Fee That Refuses to Go Away

A six-figure charge on H-1B visa petitions is back in the spotlight. After a federal judge blocked the Trump administration's attempt to impose a $103,265 fee on new H-1B applications, officials responded this week by publishing a formal rule aimed at putting the same price tag into law through the standard regulatory process. The move opens a 30-day public comment period, giving businesses, workers, universities and advocacy groups a chance to weigh in before the rule can be finalized.

The H-1B program allows U.S. employers to hire foreign workers in "specialty occupations" that typically require a bachelor's degree or higher, and it has long been a key hiring channel for technology companies, hospitals, universities and research labs. A fee approaching six figures per petition would mark one of the most significant changes to the program's cost structure in its history.

## What the Rule Actually Does

According to the filing, the proposed regulation would require many H-1B petitioners to pay $103,265 as part of the application process, a figure the administration has tied to broader efforts to prioritize higher-wage, higher-skill hiring and to discourage what it describes as the underpayment of visa holders relative to U.S. workers in similar roles. Supporters of the approach argue that a substantial fee could reduce the volume of lower-wage petitions and push employers toward hiring workers at wages closer to market rates.

Because the administration's earlier attempt to impose the fee through executive action was halted in court, the new filing follows the formal notice-and-comment rulemaking process. That means the public, including affected companies and workers, now has a window to submit feedback before the Department of Homeland Security or related agencies can move toward a final rule. Comments filed during this period can influence the final wording, exemptions or implementation timeline, and the rule could still face legal challenges after it is finalized.

## Who Could Feel It Most

Industries that rely heavily on the H-1B program are watching closely. Technology firms have used the visa category for years to fill roles in software engineering, data science and other specialized fields. Hospitals and health systems, particularly in areas facing physician and specialist shortages, have used H-1B sponsorship to recruit doctors and researchers. Universities and research institutions similarly depend on the visa to bring in scientists, postdoctoral researchers and academic specialists from abroad.

A fee in the six-figure range would represent a major new cost for smaller employers and startups in particular, which typically have thinner margins than large multinational corporations. Larger companies with bigger hiring budgets may be better positioned to absorb the cost, potentially widening the gap between which employers can realistically sponsor international talent.

## The Debate Ahead

Business groups and immigration attorneys have signaled they are likely to submit comments during the 30-day window, and some have suggested the size of the fee could still be challenged in court even after the rule is finalized, given the earlier judicial setback. Advocates for stricter immigration controls have generally welcomed higher costs as a way to ensure the program is used for genuinely specialized, high-wage roles rather than as a lower-cost alternative to domestic hiring.

Critics, including some employer associations and worker advocacy groups, have raised concerns that a flat fee of this size does not account for differences between industries, company sizes or regions, and that it could disproportionately affect nonprofit research institutions, hospitals and smaller tech firms that do not have the same resources as major corporations.

## What Happens Next

With the comment period now open, the coming weeks are expected to bring a wave of formal submissions from employers, universities, unions and legal experts. The administration will be required to review and respond to substantive comments before issuing a final rule, a process that can take additional weeks or months depending on the volume and complexity of feedback received.

For now, employers planning to sponsor H-1B workers are being advised by immigration attorneys to monitor the rulemaking process closely, since the outcome could affect hiring budgets, timelines and strategy well into the next visa cycle. Whether the $103,265 figure survives the comment period intact, or is adjusted before finalization, is likely to become clearer only after the public comment window closes and regulators issue their response.
